slides.heading: Naming Variables
slides.body: Naming Variables is part of Variables and Primitive Data Types. This short lesson gives you a practical Python idea you can understand, try, and reuse in simple programs.

slides.heading: Core Idea: Naming Variables
slides.body: Variable names should be clear and follow Python rules. Good names make code easier to read and maintain.

slides.heading: Real-World Analogy
slides.body: Naming a variable is like labeling a folder. A clear label helps you know what is inside without opening it.

annotations.note: This line stores or updates a value using a variable.
This line displays a value or message on the screen.

slides.heading: Key Rule
slides.body: Use clear variable names and match the data type to the kind of value you need to store.

slides.heading: Try It Yourself!
slides.prompt: Create a clear variable name for a favorite food, then print it.
slides.hint: Use lowercase words separated by underscores, such as favorite_food.

quiz.prompt_text: Which of the following is an example of a good Python variable name?
quiz.explanation: Well done! favorite_food follows Python naming rules: lowercase letters, no spaces (use underscores instead), and does not start with a number.

quiz.prompt_text: Arrange the following lines in the correct order to create a clearly named variable and print it.

lines: # Name a variable for a favorite food

quiz.explanation: The comment comes first, then the variable is defined with a clear name, and finally it is printed.

quiz.prompt_text: Create a variable with a clear name for your favorite color and print it.

content.starter_code: # Choose a clear variable name below
content.hint: Use lowercase and underscores for multi-word names, like favorite_color = "blue".

quiz.correct_answer: Any valid Python code that satisfies the prompt.
quiz.explanation: A name like favorite_color = "blue" followed by print(favorite_color) is clear and readable.
